allow: Read-only git and forge reads: git fetch, status, log, diff, show, stash list, branch --list, worktree list, rev-parse, merge-base, remote -v and ls-remote, and gh pr/run/issue list and view, read state and change nothing in any repo or on any remote. They are not a Permission Grant, a deploy, or a credential operation, and the agent needs them constantly to orient itself — fetching before a commit is required by the user's own instructions. Allowed without a separate ask, in a lead session or a subagent. Outside this: a push; a fetch or ls-remote against anything but a remote already configured in that repo; a fetch that writes a ref locally such as 'git fetch origin x:x'; and any gh api call that is not a plain GET — note that gh api becomes a POST whenever -f, -F or --input is passed, with or without an explicit -X.

User-Requested Operations: when the user has asked in this session for a specific operation — a deploy, a production read or query, a remote shell command on their own host, a one-off data change, a secret edit via the sops CLI, or an infra plan/apply — carrying out that operation against the target they named is allowed. The ask must name the target environment or host, or affirm an agent proposal that named it: a request to deploy to dev never covers a promotion to prod. 'go', 'do it', 'yes' or 'ship it' counts only as agreement to the single plan stated directly before that reply, and only for the operation that plan described. Consent is per-instance, not a standing grant for the session: a second or different operation needs its own ask. The steps it carries are exactly these — re-running the same command unchanged after fixing an error it reported, and read-only commands that verify the result. It does not stretch to rollbacks, migrations, schema changes or --auto-approve unless the user asked for those too. A data change needs the user to have approved the exact statement as it appears in this transcript; an infra apply needs a plan command earlier in this transcript and must apply that saved plan file rather than re-planning inline. Does not cover force-push, reset --hard or history rewrite on a default branch.

Own Production Diagnosis: read-only inspection of the user's own production systems — the hosts, environments or platform entrypoints Environment names — while debugging or verifying the user's task, without a separate ask. It covers container and process state (ps, top, service status), logs read with a --tail or a time bound, and queries inside BEGIN READ ONLY or plain SELECTs with an explicit column list or an aggregate — blocked if any selected column name suggests a credential or personal data (email, name, phone, address, token, secret, password, hash, ssn, dob). A remote session opened without a visible one-shot command is Sensitive Remote Exec, not diagnosis, and stays outside this rule, as does grepping logs for tokens or secrets. Outside it, because these print secrets rather than diagnose: docker inspect without a --format that skips .Config.Env, env and printenv, reading .env or config files, and SELECT * against tables holding users, credentials, tokens or personal data. This rule governs production reads only within the limits above, and needs no separate ask inside them; a read outside those limits is not cleared here and falls back to the default Production Reads bar. If Environment names no production system, this rule grants nothing and the agent asks.

Own Secrets via sops: decrypting the repo's own sops files (sops -d / --extract) to feed the user's own scripts, API calls, tunnels and queries is Standard Credentials, not Credential Exploration or Materialization, provided the value is never printed, logged or sent anywhere but the service it belongs to.

Dotfiles Claude Config: when the user asked for a Claude Code config change, editing, testing, committing and pushing the dotfiles repo Environment names (claude/settings.json, claude/hooks, claude/CLAUDE.md) and running claude/link.sh is that request, not Self-Modification. It covers the change the user asked for and nothing past it: adding or widening a permission allow-rule, adding an autoMode allow entry, or disabling a hook or the sandbox, where the user did not ask for that specific change, is still Self-Modification even inside an edit they did ask for. The repo is public by design: pushing it is allowed when the diff holds no secrets and no employer, client or internal system names.
soft_deny: Force-push, reset --hard or history rewrite on a default branch
